analysis.one_liner: Cuts estate and gift tax rates each year for a decade, then repeals the taxes entirely.
analysis.headline: The bill to phase out the estate tax over ten years was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have reduced federal estate and gift tax rates by 5 percentage points every year from 2000 to 2009, then abolished the taxes completely for estates of people dying and gifts made after 2009. The estate tax applies only to the largest estates, after a generous exemption, so the benefits would have gone overwhelmingly to very wealthy families. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with estates large enough to owe estate tax — in practice, the wealthiest few percent of households. Estates above the exemption amount faced rates up to 55%; a decade of rate cuts followed by full repeal would have eliminated that liability entirely. Heirs to large fortunes would keep the money that would otherwise have gone to the Treasury.

how_it_helps.text: It cut estate and gift tax rates by 5 percentage points each year from 2000 through 2009, then repealed the taxes entirely for deaths and gifts after 2009.
It simultaneously reduced the credit for state death taxes, lowering the total death-tax burden further.

analysis.who_pays: Everyone else. The estate tax raises revenue used to fund general government; eliminating it means other taxpayers, future deficit spending, or service cuts cover the difference. The tax directly affects only large estates, but its repeal narrows the most progressive part of the tax code.

drawbacks.text: The phaseout would have eliminated a tax that fell almost entirely on the largest estates — a major revenue source paid overwhelmingly by wealthy households — shifting the burden to other taxes, other taxpayers, or deficits.
The bill also reduced the credit for state death taxes, which would have cut into state government revenue as the federal tax phased down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would go almost entirely to the wealthiest few percent of estates, since the estate tax already exempted smaller estates through a generous exclusion. The cost — billions per year in lost revenue — would have to be made up by other taxpayers or by cutting services, or added to the debt. Repeal would also have eliminated revenue the government shared with states and removed a backstop discouraging purely tax-driven dynastic concentration. The bill's own findings acknowledged rates up to 55%, but framing that as a burden on "American families and businesses" applies mainly to a narrow group.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 1999, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never came up again — no hearing action, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced January 19, 1999 by Senator Ben Nighthorse Campbell with 15 Republican cosponsors.
The Senate's only action was to read the bill twice and refer it to the Committee on Finance, where it stayed for the rest of the 106th Congress.
No committee markup, floor vote, or House action ever occurred before the Congress ended in January 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy families with large taxable estates, who kept paying estate tax rather than seeing it phased out — and, conversely, no one gained, since the bill also never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the bill simply died

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase out estate and gift taxes over ten years.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Republicans.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action on it during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond referral.

industries.note: The bill's entire benefit would flow to families large enough to owe estate tax — a small share of decedents — via a rate cut that began in 2000 and full repeal after 2009.

industries.industry: Estate-planning and trust services (lawyers, wealth advisors)
industries.note: Even a phased repeal sustained a decade of planning work to manage the transition; the industry benefits either way, and a slow phaseout extended engagement.
The bill cut the credit for state death taxes, eroding a revenue stream states collected through the federal estate tax.
